lessons.title: Definition and Scope

cards.title: Definition and Scope
cards.body: Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computers, networks, and data from unauthorized access and digital attacks. Just like you lock your house to prevent theft, cybersecurity uses digital locks and protections to keep your information safe.

cards.title: Real World Example
cards.body: When you shop on Amazon and enter your credit card number, cybersecurity protects that information from hackers who might steal it and misuse it.

cards.title: Why It Matters
cards.body: Without cybersecurity, your personal photos, passwords, bank accounts, and private messages could be stolen or deleted by criminals. Your entire digital life would be at risk.

cards.title: Key Takeaway
cards.body: Cybersecurity is about keeping the bad actors out and ensuring only trusted people can access your information.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computers, networks, and data from unauthorized access and digital attacks. Just like you lock your house to prevent theft, cybersecurity uses digital locks and protections to keep your information safe.

lessons.title: The CIA Triad - Three Pillars of Security

cards.title: The CIA Triad - Three Pillars of Security
cards.body: Every security system is built on three fundamental principles. Understanding CIA Triad helps you see how security protects you from different angles.

cards.title: Confidentiality
cards.body:
**Confidentiality**

Definition: Only authorized people should see the data

Example: Your Instagram password should only be known by you. If someone else knows it, your confidentiality is broken.

Real Scenario: A company keeps employee salaries confidential. Only HR and finance teams can see it, not the entire office.

cards.title: Integrity
cards.body:
**Integrity**

Definition: Data should not be changed without permission

Example: When you check your exam results online, those scores should remain exactly as the teacher entered them. If someone changes 45 to 95 without permission, integrity is broken.

Real Scenario: A hospital patient's medical records must not be altered by unauthorized people. Changing a blood type could harm the patient.

cards.title: Availability
cards.body:
**Availability**

Definition: Authorized people should be able to access data when they need it

Example: If Gmail is down for maintenance, you cannot access your emails. This is an availability problem.

Real Scenario: During exam season, if the school's result server crashes, students cannot check their marks when needed.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
options: The CIA Triad - Three Pillars of Security
quiz.explanation: Every security system is built on three fundamental principles. Understanding CIA Triad helps you see how security protects you from different angles.

lessons.title: Common Threats

cards.title: Common Threats
cards.body: These are the most common ways attackers try to harm you. Knowing them helps you avoid falling victim.

cards.title: Malware
cards.body:
**Malware**

Software designed to damage or disable your computer or steal information from it

Real Example: You download what looks like a free game, but it actually contains code that records every keystroke you type. Now the attacker knows your passwords, credit card numbers, and private messages.

How it Spreads: Infected email attachments, cracked software downloads, fake antivirus programs

Warning Sign: Your computer runs slowly, strange pop-ups appear, or files go missing

cards.title: Phishing
cards.body:
**Phishing**

Fake messages or links designed to trick you into giving away passwords or personal information

Real Example: You receive an email saying 'Your Amazon account is locked! Verify here.' You click the link, enter your password on a fake website, and the attacker now has access to your real Amazon account and can buy things using your money.

How it Spreads: Fake emails, WhatsApp messages, SMS texts, fake websites that look identical to real ones

Warning Sign: Email from a 'trusted' source asking you to verify passwords or update payment information

cards.title: Ransomware
cards.body:
**Ransomware**

Malware that locks your files and demands payment to unlock them

Real Example: A school principal receives an email with 'Exam_Results_2024.pdf'. She opens it thinking it's legitimate. Suddenly, all files on the school's computer get encrypted and a message appears: 'Pay $5000 in Bitcoin or your files are gone forever.'

How it Spreads: Email attachments, suspicious downloads, compromised websites

Warning Sign: Locked files with a message demanding payment

cards.title: Social Engineering
cards.body:
**Social Engineering**

Using manipulation and deception to trick people into revealing confidential information

Real Example: You receive a call: 'Hi, this is your bank calling. We need to verify your account. Can you give us your One-Time Password (OTP)?' You trust the caller voice and share the OTP. Now the attacker can access your bank account.

How it Spreads: Phone calls pretending to be from banks, fake emails from 'support teams', impersonation on social media

Warning Sign: Urgent requests for passwords, OTPs, or personal information over the phone

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: These are the most common ways attackers try to harm you. Knowing them helps you avoid falling victim.

lessons.title: Attack Vectors - How Attackers Gain Access

cards.title: Attack Vectors - How Attackers Gain Access
cards.body: An attack vector is the path or method an attacker uses to reach their target. Just like a burglar chooses between a window, door, or roof to enter a house, attackers have multiple ways to target you.

cards.title: Email
cards.body:
**Email**

Sending malicious links or infected files through email

Example: An email arrives saying 'You've won an iPhone!' with a link. When you click it, malware downloads to your computer.

Prevention: Never click links or download attachments from unknown senders

cards.title: Network/Internet
cards.body:
**Network/Internet**

Exploiting unencrypted networks or hacking into WiFi to intercept data

Example: You connect to free WiFi at an airport. An attacker sitting nearby has hacked into that network and can see all passwords and credit card information you type.

Prevention: Avoid using public WiFi for sensitive activities like banking

cards.title: Physical Access
cards.body:
**Physical Access**

Gaining direct access to a computer or device to steal data or install malware

Example: Someone leaves their laptop unattended in a cafe. A thief sits down, plugs in a USB drive, and copies all the files.

Prevention: Never leave your devices unattended in public places

cards.title: Social Media
cards.body:
**Social Media**

Using social platforms to gather information or trick people into revealing secrets

Example: A fake Facebook profile claims to be your friend and asks you to share your mother's maiden name for 'verification'. This is often used as a security question for password recovery.

Prevention: Be cautious about what information you share publicly online

cards.title: USB/External Devices
cards.body:
**USB/External Devices**

Infected USB drives or devices left in public places to trick people into plugging them in

Example: Someone leaves a USB drive in the parking lot labeled 'Salary Information.xlsx'. When an employee plugs it in to check what's inside, malware instantly infects the office network.

Prevention: Never plug in unknown USB devices or external drives

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
options: Attack Vectors - How Attackers Gain Access
quiz.explanation: An attack vector is the path or method an attacker uses to reach their target. Just like a burglar chooses between a window, door, or roof to enter a house, attackers have multiple ways to target you.

lessons.title: Defense-in-Depth - Layered Security

cards.title: Defense-in-Depth - Layered Security
cards.body: Defense-in-depth means using multiple layers of security instead of relying on just one. If one layer fails, others still protect you. Think of a castle with a moat, outer wall, inner wall, and guards - multiple obstacles to slow down attackers.

cards.title: Layer 1 - Physical Security
cards.body:
**Layer 1 - Physical Security**

Locks, security cameras, guards, and restricted access

Example: Your office building has key card access - only employees can enter

cards.title: Layer 2 - Perimeter Security
cards.body:
**Layer 2 - Perimeter Security**

Firewalls and network security to block unwanted traffic

Example: Your WiFi router requires a password. Without it, strangers cannot connect

cards.title: Layer 3 - Application Security
cards.body:
**Layer 3 - Application Security**

Software protections like antivirus and encryption

Example: Banking apps encrypt your password so even the bank cannot see it in plain text

cards.title: Layer 4 - Data Security
cards.body:
**Layer 4 - Data Security**

Backups, encryption, and secure storage

Example: Your photos are backed up to cloud storage so you don't lose them if your phone breaks

cards.title: Layer 5 - User Education
cards.body:
**Layer 5 - User Education**

Teaching people to recognize threats and practice good habits

Example: Companies train employees to not click suspicious links or share passwords

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: Defense-in-depth means using multiple layers of security instead of relying on just one. If one layer fails, others still protect you. Think of a castle with a moat, outer wall, inner wall, and guards - multiple obstacles to slow down attackers.

lessons.title: Practical Activity - Identify Threats in a Mock Organization

cards.title: Scenario
cards.body: TechStart is a 50-person company that creates mobile apps. Here's what happens one day: An HR manager receives an email saying 'Update your employee benefits here' with a link. She clicks it and enters her password. The same morning, an employee downloads cracked software to avoid buying a license. A customer's USB drive is found in the parking lot with 'Customer Database' written on it. The company doesn't have a firewall, and employees use the same WiFi password for a month.

cards.title: Practical Activity - Identify Threats in a Mock Organization
cards.body: Let's apply what we learned. Below is a scenario of a small company. Identify the security problems and explain how each attack vector is being exploited.

cards.title: What security threats does TechStart face?
cards.body:
**Answer:**
1. Phishing attack on HR manager - social engineering vector. 2. Malware from cracked software - dangerous download. 3. Physical attack vector - USB drive in parking lot. 4. Weak network security - no firewall and shared password.

cards.title: Which CIA Triad principle is violated in each threat?
cards.body:
**Answer:**
1. Phishing: Confidentiality (password exposed). 2. Cracked software: Integrity (files can be modified). 3. USB drive: Confidentiality (data exposed). 4. Weak WiFi: All three principles at risk.

cards.title: How can TechStart use defense-in-depth to prevent this?
cards.body:
**Answer:**
Install a firewall, require strong passwords, train employees about phishing, use antivirus software, back up data, implement multi-factor authentication, secure the office entrance, and change WiFi password regularly.

options: Practical Activity - Identify Threats in a Mock Organization
quiz.explanation: Let's apply what we learned. Below is a scenario of a small company. Identify the security problems and explain how each attack vector is being exploited.

lessons.title: Operating System Basics - Windows, macOS, Linux

cards.title: Operating System Basics - Windows, macOS, Linux
cards.body: An Operating System (OS) is the software that controls your computer. Windows, macOS, and Linux are the three most common OSes. Each has its own security features you need to understand.

cards.title: Windows
cards.body:
**Windows**

Most personal computers and businesses use Windows

Security: Built-in Defender antivirus, Windows Defender Firewall

Common on: Laptops, desktops, some servers

cards.title: macOS
cards.body:
**macOS**

Apple computers, many designers and developers

Security: Gatekeeper (prevents unauthorized apps), XProtect (malware detection)

Common on: MacBooks, iMacs, Mac Minis

cards.title: Linux
cards.body:
**Linux**

Servers, developers, security experts, and tech-savvy users

Security: Built-in permissions system, no single point of vulnerability

Common on: Web servers, cloud systems, Android phones underneath

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
options: Operating System Basics - Windows, macOS, Linux
quiz.explanation: An Operating System (OS) is the software that controls your computer. Windows, macOS, and Linux are the three most common OSes. Each has its own security features you need to understand.

lessons.title: File Permissions and Access Control

cards.title: File Permissions and Access Control
cards.body: File permissions control who can read, write, or execute files. Think of them as rules on a file that say 'Who is allowed to do what with this file?'

cards.title: Real World Example
cards.body: In Windows, your Documents folder has Read and Write permissions for you. Your friend's computer cannot access it because they don't have permissions. A malware trying to modify system files will fail because it doesn't have Write permission.

cards.title: Why It Matters
cards.body: Without proper permissions, a hacker could read your private documents, modify important system files, or delete everything on your computer.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: File permissions control who can read, write, or execute files. Think of them as rules on a file that say 'Who is allowed to do what with this file?'

lessons.title: User Accounts and Access Control

cards.title: User Accounts and Access Control
cards.body: User accounts are identities on a computer. Each account has different permission levels. The OS uses accounts to track who did what and to enforce security rules.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: User accounts are identities on a computer. Each account has different permission levels. The OS uses accounts to track who did what and to enforce security rules.

cards.title: User Authentication - Passwords
cards.body: Authentication is proving you are who you claim to be. The most common method is a password - a secret code only you know.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: Authentication is proving you are who you claim to be. The most common method is a password - a secret code only you know.

cards.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
cards.body: MFA adds a second layer of verification beyond just your password. Even if someone steals your password, they still cannot access your account without the second factor.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: MFA adds a second layer of verification beyond just your password. Even if someone steals your password, they still cannot access your account without the second factor.

lessons.title: Account Management - Principle of Least Privilege

cards.title: Account Management - Principle of Least Privilege
cards.body: Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) means giving people only the minimum permissions they need to do their job. Nothing more, nothing less.

cards.title: Why It Matters
cards.body: If an account gets hacked, attackers can only do what that account is allowed to do. Limited permissions = limited damage.

quiz.explanation: Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) means giving people only the minimum permissions they need to do their job. Nothing more, nothing less.

lessons.title: Network Basics - TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP, and Ports

cards.title: Network Basics - TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP, and Ports
cards.body: A network is a collection of connected computers sharing data. To understand network security, you need to know the basics of how computers communicate.

cards.title: TCP/IP Protocol
cards.body:
**TCP/IP Protocol**

TCP/IP is the set of rules that computers use to communicate over the internet. Think of it as the language computers speak to each other.

Real Example: When you send a WhatsApp message, your phone breaks it into tiny pieces (packets). Each packet has your IP address and the recipient's IP address. The packets travel through the internet and get reassembled on the other end.

Security Note: Without encryption, someone on your network could intercept these packets and read your messages or steal data.

cards.title: DNS (Domain Name System)
cards.body:
**DNS (Domain Name System)**

DNS translates human-readable website names into IP addresses that computers understand.

Real Example: You visit Facebook.com. Behind the scenes, your computer queries a DNS server to find Facebook's actual IP address, then connects to it.

Security Risk: DNS spoofing: An attacker can intercept DNS queries and give you the wrong IP address. You think you're visiting your bank, but you're actually on a fake website controlled by the attacker.

Protection: Use secure DNS services like Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) or Google DNS (8.8.8.8) instead of your ISP's DNS.

cards.title: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)
cards.body:
**DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)**

DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses to devices on a network. Without DHCP, you'd have to manually type in IP addresses for every device.

Real Example: You bring your laptop to a coffee shop and connect to their WiFi. DHCP gives your laptop a temporary IP address so you can browse the internet.

Security Risk: Rogue DHCP server: An attacker sets up a fake DHCP server that hands out IP addresses and routes all your traffic through their computer. They can see everything you do.

Protection: Connect only to trusted networks. Use VPN on public WiFi.

cards.title: Ports
cards.body:
**Ports**

Ports are like doors on your computer. Different services use different ports. Port 80 is for websites (HTTP), Port 443 is for secure websites (HTTPS), Port 25 is for email.

Real Example: When you visit www.google.com, your browser connects to port 443 on Google's server. Google's web server listens on port 443 and responds with the website.

Security Risk: Open ports are entry points. If port 3306 (MySQL) is open to the internet, attackers can try to hack into the database.

Protection: Close unnecessary ports. Use firewalls to block dangerous ports. Only open ports that are needed for your services.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
options: Network Basics - TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP, and Ports
quiz.explanation: A network is a collection of connected computers sharing data. To understand network security, you need to know the basics of how computers communicate.

lessons.title: Network Segmentation - VLANs and Isolating Critical Systems

cards.title: Network Segmentation - VLANs and Isolating Critical Systems
cards.body: Network segmentation means dividing a network into smaller, isolated sections. If one section is breached, attackers cannot easily access other sections.

body.vlan_1: Customer service area - employees using computers to help customers. VLAN can access public data only.
body.vlan_2: Finance department - handles sensitive financial data. Encrypted and heavily protected.
body.vlan_3: IT and servers - critical systems. Very restricted access.
body.vlan_4: Guest WiFi - for visitors. Completely isolated from everything else.
body.benefit: If a visitor's infected laptop connects to guest WiFi, it cannot reach the bank's sensitive data. The malware is confined to the guest network.

cards.title: Why It Matters
cards.body: Imagine a hospital where doctors, patients, administrative staff, and IT equipment are all on the same network. If a patient's laptop gets infected with malware, it could spread to the entire hospital, including critical systems. With segmentation, the patient network is isolated.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
options: Network Segmentation - VLANs and Isolating Critical Systems
quiz.explanation: Network segmentation means dividing a network into smaller, isolated sections. If one section is breached, attackers cannot easily access other sections.

cards.title: Firewalls and Routers - Stateful vs. Stateless Filtering
cards.body: A firewall is a security system that filters network traffic. There are two main filtering approaches: stateless and stateful. Understanding the difference is crucial for network security.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?

lessons.title: Intrusion Detection - IDS/IPS Concepts

cards.title: Intrusion Detection - IDS/IPS Concepts
cards.body: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) monitors network traffic for suspicious activity. An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) does the same thing but can also block attacks automatically.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) monitors network traffic for suspicious activity. An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) does the same thing but can also block attacks automatically.

lessons.title: VPN Basics - Encryption in Transit and Remote Access Security

cards.title: VPN Basics - Encryption in Transit and Remote Access Security
cards.body: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) is a secure tunnel through the internet. All your traffic is encrypted and routed through a VPN server, hiding your identity and protecting your data.

body.scenario: You're working from a coffee shop and need to access your company's internal files
body.without_vpn: You connect directly to the cafe WiFi. The attacker intercepts your traffic, sees you logging into your company account, and steals your password.
body.with_vpn: You connect to the cafe WiFi and then connect to your company's VPN. All traffic is encrypted. The attacker only sees encrypted packets and cannot read anything.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
options: VPN Basics - Encryption in Transit and Remote Access Security
quiz.explanation: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) is a secure tunnel through the internet. All your traffic is encrypted and routed through a VPN server, hiding your identity and protecting your data.

lessons.title: Symmetric Encryption - AES

cards.title: Symmetric Encryption - AES
cards.body: Symmetric encryption means using the same key to both encrypt and decrypt data. It's like a lock where the same key locks and unlocks the door.

body.scenario: A bank encrypts customer account data at rest (stored on hard drives)
body.process: All customer data is encrypted using AES-256. The encryption key is stored in a secure Hardware Security Module (HSM). Even if someone steals the hard drive, the data is encrypted and useless without the key.
body.benefit: If a bank gets hacked, the attacker gets encrypted data, not readable customer information.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: Symmetric encryption means using the same key to both encrypt and decrypt data. It's like a lock where the same key locks and unlocks the door.

lessons.title: Asymmetric Encryption - RSA

cards.title: Asymmetric Encryption - RSA
cards.body: Asymmetric encryption uses two different keys: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption. Unlike symmetric, you don't need to share the decryption key.

body.scenario: Sending a secure email to a bank
process: The bank publishes its public key on their website
You download the bank's public key
You type your sensitive information and encrypt it with the bank's public key
The encrypted message is sent over the internet
Even if a hacker intercepts it, they only have the encrypted message and the public key. They cannot decrypt it.
The bank receives the message and decrypts it with their private key (which only they have)
Only the bank can read your sensitive information

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: Asymmetric encryption uses two different keys: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption. Unlike symmetric, you don't need to share the decryption key.

lessons.title: Hashing - MD5, SHA-256, and Why It's Different

cards.title: Hashing - MD5, SHA-256, and Why It's Different
cards.body: Hashing is NOT encryption. A hash function converts any data into a fixed-size string of characters. The process is one-way - you cannot reverse it to get the original data.

lessons.title: Digital Signatures - Authentication and Non-repudiation

cards.title: Digital Signatures - Authentication and Non-repudiation
cards.body: A digital signature proves that you created or approved a document. It's like your handwritten signature on a paper contract, but for digital documents.

quiz.question: What was the main concept discussed in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: A digital signature proves that you created or approved a document. It's like your handwritten signature on a paper contract, but for digital documents.

lessons.title: SSL/TLS - HTTPS and Secure Web Communication

cards.title: SSL/TLS - HTTPS and Secure Web Communication
cards.body: SSL/TLS is a protocol that encrypts communication between your browser and a website. When you see the padlock icon on a website, that's SSL/TLS at work.

body.scenario: Logging into your bank account on public WiFi
body.with_http: Your password is sent in plaintext. A hacker on the WiFi captures it immediately. They access your bank account.
body.with_https: Your password is encrypted with SSL/TLS. Hacker on WiFi sees only encrypted gibberish. Cannot read your password. Your account is safe.

options: SSL/TLS - HTTPS and Secure Web Communication
quiz.explanation: SSL/TLS is a protocol that encrypts communication between your browser and a website. When you see the padlock icon on a website, that's SSL/TLS at work.

lessons.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

cards.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
cards.body: CSRF tricks users into performing unwanted actions on a website where they're already logged in. The attacker doesn't see the response, but the action is performed.
